question: PFAS contamination and the protection of mothers

While the Committee for Socio-Economic Analysis (SEAC) of the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) continues to assess over 3 500 submissions received during the consultation on the proposed restriction on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), new evidence continues to demonstrate the scale and persistence of PFAS contamination.

For instance, the Dutch National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM) recently detected PFAS in all breast milk samples analysed from 1 629 women. In 18 % of cases, concentrations exceeded the health-based guidance value, suggesting exposure levels that may negatively affect health. RIVM has warned that excessive PFAS exposure in infants may impair immune system function. 1.

Does the Commission recognise that each additional derogation from a PFAS restriction prolongs contamination of Europe’s water, soil and food chains, while imposing the costs of remediation and related health and environmental impacts on society rather than on polluters?

When considering derogations, will the Commission ensure that the costs associated with PFAS pollution and the resulting impacts, including any necessary remediation, are borne by polluters, in line with the ‘polluter pays’ principle and consistent with the approach reflected in the Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive?
While the restriction process is ongoing, what further measures will the Commission take to protect pregnant women, infants and other vulnerable groups from continued PFAS exposure?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.10.2026) As indicated in the European Chemicals Industry Action Plan1, the Commission is considering a per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) ban in consumer uses such as cosmetics, food contact materials and outdoor clothing.

Where adequate alternatives in terms of performance and safety are not available, the continued use of PFAS in industrial applications may be allowed for critical applications under strict conditions until acceptable substitutes are found.

Derogations for uses will need to be accompanied by requirements to reduce emissions at all lifecycle stages to limit the release of pollutants into the environment and by clear incentives to innovate. The Commission will also address existing PFAS pollution by promoting EU-wide monitoring to improve data collection, information sharing and promote clean-up efforts.

Cleanup should be based on the polluter pays principle, with public money allocated to clean up orphan sites, where no liable entity could be found. With a view of protecting human health, including pregnant women and their unborn children, Regulation (EU) 2023/9152 sets maximum levels (MLs) in certain foods of animal origin for the four main PFAS that are currently observed in food and human blood.

Furthermore, the new occurrence data on PFAS in food that have been collected under Recommendation (EU) 2022/14313 are currently being compiled by the European Food Safety Authority and will be used, to assess whether MLs should be established for additional foods or if certain current MLs should be lowered.
